claim: Arl3 is a member of the ADP-ribosylation factor (Arf) family of small GTPases that are important for membrane trafficking.
source: Arl3 is a member of the ADP-ribosylation factor (Arf) family of small GTPases that are important for membrane trafficking (Cavenagh et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cavenagh et al., 1994

claim: Arl3 is ubiquitously expressed in ciliated cells where it regulates the ciliary enrichment of lipidated proteins.
source: Arl3 is ubiquitously expressed in ciliated cells where it regulates the ciliary enrichment of lipidated proteins (Fansa and Wittinghofer, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fansa and Wittinghofer, 2016

claim: Many prenylated and myristoylated proteins are shuttled by the Arl3 effectors PDEδ and UNC119A/B, respectively.
source: Many prenylated and myristoylated proteins are shuttled by the Arl3 effectors PDEδ and UNC119A/B, respectively (Fansa et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fansa et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2004

claim: PDEδ and UNC119A/B are chaperones that sequester the lipid anchor moiety of proteins within an intramolecular cavity to enable detachment of these proteins from membranes.
source: PDEδ and UNC119A/B are chaperones that sequester the lipid anchor moiety of proteins within an intramolecular cavity to enable detachment of these proteins from membranes (Hanzal-Bayer et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hanzal-Bayer et al., 2002

claim: Arl3 is specifically activated in the cilium by its guanine exchange factor (GEF) Arl13B and co-GEF BART.
source: Arl3 is specifically activated in the cilium by its guanine exchange factor (GEF) Arl13B and co-GEF BART (ElMaghloob et al., 2021; Gotthardt et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to ElMaghloob et al., 2021; Gotthardt et al., 2015

claim: Active GTP-bound Arl3 binds to the chaperones allowing them to unload their lipidated cargo at the cilium.
source: Active GTP-bound Arl3 then binds to the chaperones allowing them to unload their lipidated cargo at the cilium.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of Arl3 function and citations in surrounding text

claim: Arl3 is inactive outside the cilium as it is inactivated by RP2, its GTPase activating protein (GAP).
source: Arl3 is inactive outside the cilium as it is inactivated by RP2, its GTPase activating protein (GAP) (Veltel et al., 2008a; Veltel et al., 2008b)
evidence: Supported by citations to Veltel et al., 2008a; Veltel et al., 2008b

claim: RP2 is found enriched at the base of the cilium, although it is also present at other locations in the cell.
source: RP2, its GTPase activating protein (GAP) (Veltel et al., 2008a; Veltel et al., 2008b) that is found enriched at the base of the cilium, although it is also present at other locations in the cell (Evans et al., 2010; Holopainen et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Evans et al., 2010; Holopainen et al., 2010

claim: Germline Arl3 knockout mice have phenotypes generally associated with human ciliopathies, including polycystic kidneys and photoreceptor degeneration.
source: Germline Arl3 knockout mice have phenotypes generally associated with human ciliopathies, including polycystic kidneys and photoreceptor degeneration (Schrick et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schrick et al., 2006

claim: In photoreceptors, Arl3 regulates enrichment of many lipidated proteins essential for eliciting the visual response within the outer segment, a modified primary cilium.
source: In photoreceptors, Arl3 regulates enrichment of many lipidated proteins essential for eliciting the visual response within the outer segment, a modified primary cilium (reviewed in Frederick et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Frederick et al., 2020

claim: Human mutation R99I in Arl3 causes autosomal recessive cone-rod dystrophy.
source: R99I causes autosomal recessive cone-rod dystrophy (Sheikh et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to Sheikh et al., 2019

claim: Human mutations R149H or R149C in Arl3 cause recessive Joubert syndrome.
source: R149H or R149C cause recessive Joubert syndrome (Alkanderi et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to Alkanderi et al., 2018

claim: Compound heterozygous T31A/C118F in Arl3 causes rod-cone dystrophy.
source: compound heterozygous T31A/C118F causes rod-cone dystrophy (Fu et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citation to Fu et al., 2021

claim: Human mutation Y90C in Arl3 causes autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa.
source: Y90C causes autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa (Holtan et al., 2019; Strom et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Holtan et al., 2019; Strom et al., 2016

claim: Human mutation D67V in Arl3 causes autosomal dominant retinal degeneration.
source: D67V causes autosomal dominant retinal degeneration (Ratnapriya et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citation to Ratnapriya et al., 2021

claim: The Arl3 R149H/C mutation prevents Arl3 activation by Arl13B, which causes reduced enrichment of lipidated proteins in the cilium.
source: The R149H/C mutation is present at the Arl3–Arl13B interface and was shown to prevent Arl3 activation by Arl13B, which causes reduced enrichment of lipidated proteins in the cilium (Alkanderi et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alkanderi et al., 2018

claim: The Arl3 mutations C118F, Y90C, and D67V have been predicted to impair its interactions with binding partners.
source: Additionally, the Arl3 mutations C118F, Y90C, and D67V have also been predicted to impair its interactions with binding partners (Fu et al., 2021; Ratnapriya et al., 2021; Strom et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Fu et al., 2021; Ratnapriya et al., 2021; Strom et al., 2016

claim: The Arl3 mutations R99I, T31A, C118F, and Y90C are predicted to destabilize Arl3.
source: while the R991, T31A, C118F, and Y90C mutations are predicted to destabilize Arl3 (Fu et al., 2021; Holtan et al., 2019; Sheikh et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fu et al., 2021; Holtan et al., 2019; Sheikh et al., 2019

claim: Both a rod-specific Arl3 knockout mouse and a transgenic mouse overexpressing constitutively active Arl3-Q71L in rods show severe retinal degeneration by 2 months.
source: Both a rod-specific Arl3 knockout mouse or a transgenic mouse overexpressing constitutively active Arl3-Q71L in rods show severe retinal degeneration by 2 months and result in measurable effects on lipidated protein delivery to the outer segment (Hanke-Gogokhia et al., 2016; Wright et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hanke-Gogokhia et al., 2016; Wright et al., 2016

claim: Only mice with Arl3-Q71L transgenic expression in rods had a subset of rod nuclei displaced from the outer nuclear layer (ONL) into the inner nuclear layer (INL).
source: However, only mice with Arl3-Q71L transgenic expression in rods had a subset of rod nuclei displaced from the outer nuclear layer (ONL) into the inner nuclear layer (INL) (Wright et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wright et al., 2016

claim: Improper rod nuclear displacement into the INL has been observed in a RP2 knockout mouse.
source: Improper rod nuclear displacement into the INL has also been observed in a RP2 knockout mouse (Li et al., 2013; Mookherjee et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 2013; Mookherjee et al., 2015

claim: Disrupting Arl3 activity in rods could lead to a nuclear migration phenotype.
source: Improper rod nuclear displacement into the INL has also been observed in a RP2 knockout mouse (Li et al., 2013; Mookherjee et al., 2015), further suggesting that disrupting Arl3 activity in rods could lead to a nuclear migration phenotype.
evidence: Inference based on RP2 knockout data and its relationship to Arl3 activity

claim: Retinal neurons are organized into three distinct nuclear layers: the ONL, the INL, and the ganglion cell layer (GCL).
source: Retinal neurons are organized into three distinct nuclear layers (listed from apical to basal): the ONL, the INL, and the ganglion cell layer (GCL).
evidence: Established knowledge of retinal anatomy

claim: During development, all retinal neurons are born apically and then migrate to their final retinal layer where they elaborate and make connections.
source: During development, all retinal neurons are born apically and then migrate to their final retinal layer where they elaborate and make connections (Baye and Link, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Baye and Link, 2008

claim: Cone nuclei are arranged at the apical side of the ONL.
source: For cones, whose nuclei are arranged at the apical side of the ONL
evidence: Established knowledge of retinal anatomy

claim: Cone nuclear position can be influenced by knocking out RASGRF2, the GEF for the Ras/Rho/Rac family of small GTPases.
source: it is known that their nuclear position can be influenced by either knocking out RASGRF2 the GEF for the Ras/Rho/Rac family of small GTPases (Jimeno et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Jimeno et al., 2016

claim: Cone nuclear position can be influenced by altering dopamine signaling through the D4 receptor.
source: altering dopamine signaling through the D4 receptor (Tufford et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to Tufford et al., 2018

claim: Cone nuclear position can be influenced by uncoupling the nucleus from microtubules.
source: or uncoupling the nucleus from microtubules (Yu et al., 2011; Razafsky et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yu et al., 2011; Razafsky et al., 2012

claim: Microtubule coupling to the nucleus is important for rod nuclear position.
source: Less is known about how rod nuclear position is determined, but microtubule coupling to the nucleus is important.
evidence: Inference from subsequent citations about mouse models

claim: Mouse models disrupting the connection between microtubules and the nucleus have found rod nuclei mislocalized to the INL.
source: Mouse models disrupting this connection have found rod nuclei mislocalized to the INL (Yu et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Yu et al., 2011

claim: Rods undergo rapid, dynein-dependent apical nuclear translocations during the formation of the retinal nuclear layers between P0 and P8.
source: and, more recently, a study found that rods undergo rapid, dynein-dependent apical nuclear translocations during the formation of the retinal nuclear layers between P0 and P8 (Aghaizu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Aghaizu et al., 2021

claim: Wild-type Arl3-FLAG is present throughout the rod photoreceptor including within the outer segment at P21.
source: FLAG immunostaining of retinal cross-sections showed wild-type Arl3-FLAG present throughout the rod photoreceptor including, notably, within the outer segment at P21 (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Arl3-D67V-FLAG and Arl3-Y90C-FLAG expression and localization were similar to wild-type Arl3-FLAG.
source: Both Arl3-D67V-FLAG and Arl3-Y90C-FLAG expression and localization were similar to wild-type Arl3-FLAG, with perhaps a trend toward less Arl3-D67V within the outer segments although this was not quantified.
evidence: Based on observation of immunostaining data

claim: 7.4% of Arl3-D67V nuclei were mislocalized to the INL.
source: many of the Arl3-D67V and Arl3-Y90C nuclei were mislocalized to the INL (Figure 1B, C), 7.4% and 2.9% of nuclei, respectively.
evidence: Quantitative data from Figure 1B

claim: 2.9% of Arl3-Y90C nuclei were mislocalized to the INL.
source: many of the Arl3-D67V and Arl3-Y90C nuclei were mislocalized to the INL (Figure 1B, C), 7.4% and 2.9% of nuclei, respectively.
evidence: Quantitative data from Figure 1C

claim: 5.4% of Arl3-Q71L nuclei were mislocalized to the INL.
source: This nuclear displacement is similar to transgenic expression of the GTP-locked mutant Arl3-Q71L (Wright et al., 2016) and our own electroporation of Arl3-Q71L (Figure 1D), in which 5.4% of nuclei were mislocalized to the INL.
evidence: Quantitative data from Figure 1D

claim: Arl3-D67V and Arl3-Y90C nuclei localized within the ONL are predominantly displaced basally.
source: Additionally, even the Arl3-D67V and Arl3-Y90C nuclei localized within the ONL are predominantly displaced basally, while the nuclei of wild-type Arl3-FLAG rods are distributed more evenly throughout the ONL.
evidence: Based on observation of nuclear distribution data

claim: All the mutants that had rod nuclei mislocalized to the INL—D67V, Q71L, and Y90C—were positively skewed and statistically significant from wild-type.
source: All the mutants that had rod nuclei mislocalized to the INL—D67V, Q71L, and Y90C—were positively skewed and statistically significant from wild-type (Table 1).
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Table 1

claim: Overexpression of Arl3-T31N-FLAG does not cause a shift in rod nuclear position.
source: This shift in rod nuclear position was not seen with overexpression of a GDP-bound inactive mimetic, Arl3-T31N-FLAG, suggesting that increased Arl3 activity during development causes a defect in rod nuclear migration (Linari et al., 1999; Figure 1E).
evidence: Data from Figure 1E showing no migration defect

claim: Increased Arl3 activity during development causes a defect in rod nuclear migration.
source: This shift in rod nuclear position was not seen with overexpression of a GDP-bound inactive mimetic, Arl3-T31N-FLAG, suggesting that increased Arl3 activity during development causes a defect in rod nuclear migration (Linari et al., 1999; Figure 1E).
evidence: Inference from comparison of active and inactive mutants

claim: Inactive Arl3-T31N did not bind to GST-PDEδ.
source: As expected, inactive Arl3-T31N did not bind to GST-PDEδ while the constitutively active Arl3-Q71L is bound.
evidence: Data from GST-PDEδ pulldown experiment shown in Figure 2A

claim: Constitutively active Arl3-Q71L binds to GST-PDEδ.
source: As expected, inactive Arl3-T31N did not bind to GST-PDEδ while the constitutively active Arl3-Q71L is bound.
evidence: Data from GST-PDEδ pulldown experiment shown in Figure 2A

claim: Arl3-D67V was pulled down by GST-PDEδ, indicating that it is constitutively active.
source: Arl3-D67V was also pulled down by GST-PDEδ, indicating that it is constitutively active.
evidence: Data from GST-PDEδ pulldown experiment shown in Figure 2A

claim: Arl3-Y90C did not bind to GST-PDEδ, indicating that it is not constitutively active.
source: Surprisingly, however, Arl3-Y90C did not bind to GST-PDEδ, indicating that it is not constitutively active (Figure 2A).
evidence: Data from GST-PDEδ pulldown experiment shown in Figure 2A

claim: Arl3-Y90C can bind GTP when there is excess GTP in the buffer.
source: We attempted to load Arl3-Y90C with GTP by incubating Arl3-Y90C-FLAG-expressing AD-293 cell lysates with EDTA (to imitate the function of the GEF by chelating out the nucleotide coordinating Mg2+) and found that, if there is excess GTP in the buffer, Arl3-Y90C can bind GTP as measured by GST-PDEδ binding, similar to both endogenous Arl3 (as seen below in the same blot) and Arl3-FLAG (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Data from GST-PDEδ pulldown experiment with GTP loading shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Arl3-Y90C binds GTP under nucleotide exchange promoting conditions more efficiently than endogenous Arl3.
source: In fact, Arl3-Y90C binds GTP under these nucleotide exchange promoting conditions more efficiently than the endogenous Arl3 expressed by these cells.
evidence: Data from GST-PDEδ pulldown experiment comparing Arl3-Y90C to endogenous Arl3

claim: Arl3-Y90C undergoes nucleotide exchange in the presence of Mg2+ when excess GTP is added.
source: Interestingly, when excess GTP was added Arl3-Y90C also underwent nucleotide exchange in the presence of Mg2+, which blocks nucleotide exchange for endogenous Arl3 (Figure 2B) and Arl3-FLAG (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Data from GST-PDEδ pulldown experiment shown in Figure 2B

claim: Arl3-Y90C exhibits GEF-independent nucleotide exchange, a behavior described as fast cycling of a small GTPase.
source: This result indicates possible GEF-independent nucleotide exchange in Arl3-Y90C, a behavior that is often described as fast cycling of a small GTPase.
evidence: Inference from nucleotide exchange data and comparison to known fast cycling behavior

claim: Arl3-D129N behaves biochemically identical to Arl3-Y90C.
source: To confirm, we tested the behavior of Arl3-D129N (Gotthardt et al., 2015), a homologous mutant of the fast cycling Ras-D119N (Cool et al., 1999), in this assay and found it behaved biochemically identical to Arl3-Y90C (Figure 2B).
evidence: Data from GST-PDEδ pulldown experiment shown in Figure 2B

claim: 3.7% of Arl3-D129N-FLAG-expressing cells were mislocalized to the INL.
source: To confirm that this biochemical result reveals small GTPase behavior relevant to the migration phenotype, we electroporated Arl3-D129N-FLAG in mouse rod photoreceptors and found that the fast cycling Arl3-D129N replicated the Arl3-Y90C migration phenotype with 3.7% of Arl3-D129N-FLAG-expressing cells mislocalized to the INL (Figure 2C).
evidence: Quantitative data from Figure 2C

claim: The Arl3-Y90C mutation results in fast cycling behavior that causes excess Arl3 activation in vivo.
source: Together, our data suggest that the Arl3-Y90C mutation results in fast cycling behavior that causes excess Arl3 activation in vivo.
evidence: Inference from biochemical and in vivo data

claim: Arl3-Y90C binds Arl13B.
source: In Figure 3A, western blot analysis of the FLAG eluates using an anti-GFP antibody shows Arl3-Y90C binds Arl13B.
evidence: Data from co-immunoprecipitation experiment shown in Figure 3A

claim: The R149H mutation disrupts Arl3-Y90C binding to Arl13B.
source: When we introduced the R149H mutation to the Arl3-Y90C mutant, Arl13B binding was disrupted similarly to the Arl3-R149H single mutant (Figure 3A), confirming that Arl3-Y90C binding to Arl13B is at the same interface as wild-type binding.
evidence: Data from co-immunoprecipitation experiment shown in Figure 3A

claim: Increased Arl13B binding to the Arl3-Y90C mutant is due to an increased nucleotide-free state of Arl3-Y90C rather than fundamental alterations within its Arl13B-binding site.
source: This result suggests that increased Arl13B binding to the Arl3-Y90C mutant is due to an increased nucleotide-free state of Arl3-Y90C rather than fundamental alterations within its Arl13B-binding site, a conclusion supported by the continued binding of Arl3-Y90C to Arl13B after an additional T31N mutation, which decouples GTP-binding state from Arl13B-binding behavior of Arl3-Y90C.
evidence: Inference from co-immunoprecipitation data with T31N/Y90C double mutant

claim: Endogenous Arl13B remains predominantly localized to the outer segment and does not mislocalize in rods expressing Arl3-Y90C-FLAG.
source: Importantly, despite the data showing strong Arl3-Y90C binding to Arl13B, endogenous Arl13B remains predominantly localized to the outer segment and does not mislocalize in rods expressing Arl3-Y90C-FLAG (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), likely due to the palmitoylation of Arl13B (Roy et al., 2017).
evidence: Data from immunostaining shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Arl3-Y90C binding does not alter Arl13B ciliary localization.
source: The same Arl13B localization pattern was observed when Arl13B-myc was co-expressed with Arl3-Y90C confirming that Arl3-Y90C binding does not alter Arl13B ciliary localization (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Data from immunostaining shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: Co-expression of Arl3-Y90C-FLAG and Arl13B-MYC rescues the migration defect.
source: To test this, the localization of rod nuclei of cells expressing both Arl3-Y90C-FLAG and Arl13B-MYC was examined. This cell population no longer has the migration defect observed with only Arl3-Y90C-FLAG expression indicating that the migration defect is caused at least in part by Arl3-Y90C acting as a dominant negative (Figure 3B).
evidence: Data from in vivo electroporation shown in Figure 3B

claim: The migration defect is caused at least in part by Arl3-Y90C acting as a dominant negative.
source: This cell population no longer has the migration defect observed with only Arl3-Y90C-FLAG expression indicating that the migration defect is caused at least in part by Arl3-Y90C acting as a dominant negative (Figure 3B).
evidence: Inference from rescue experiment data

claim: Three major Arl3 complexes are visible in the presence of active Arl3-Q71L when DSS crosslinker is added.
source: When DSS crosslinker was added, three major Arl3 complexes were visible in the presence of active Arl3-Q71L (Figure 4A).
evidence: Data from in vivo crosslinking experiment shown in Figure 4A

claim: Mass spectrometry analysis identified RP2, UNC119, and BART as Arl3-binding partners in Arl3-Q71L but not in Arl3-T31N samples.
source: Mass spectrometry analysis of DSS treated lysates identified three known Arl3-binding partners: RP2, UNC119, and BART in the Arl3-Q71L but not in the Arl3-T31N sample (Figure 4B).
evidence: Data from mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 4B

claim: The ~65 kDa band is a complex between RP2 and Arl3-Q71L.
source: Western blot using antibodies against RP2 confirmed that the ~65 kDa band is indeed a complex between RP2 and Arl3-Q71L (Figure 4C, lane 2).
evidence: Data from western blot shown in Figure 4C

claim: The ~55 kDa band is a complex between Arl3 and UNC119A.
source: We took a similar approach to confirm that UNC119 is forming the ~55 kDa complex with Arl3-Q71L by using Arl3-D67V. This mutant has constitutive activity in our GST-PDEδ in vitro pulldowns (Figure 2A) but is unable to interact with UNC119A-myc (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). Indeed, the ~55 kDa band is strongly reduced in the presence of Arl3-D67V, confirming that this complex is between Arl3 and UNC119A (Figure 4C, lane 3).
evidence: Data from western blot shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Arl3-Y90C is active in AD-293 cells and binding effectors but is inactivated by RP2.
source: We then performed the in vivo crosslinking on cells expressing Arl3-Y90C-FLAG and found that Arl3-Y90C formed complexes with UNC119 and BART but did not make a stable complex with RP2 (Figure 4D). This result suggests that Arl3-Y90C is active in AD-293 cells and binding effectors but, unlike Arl3-Q71L, is inactivated by RP2 and therefore does not form a stable complex with RP2.
evidence: Data from in vivo crosslinking experiment shown in Figure 4D

claim: Both fast cycling mutants, Arl3-D129N and Arl3-Y90C, had significantly higher levels of effector binding than wild-type Arl3.
source: To understand the relative level of active Arl3-Y90C in cells, we measured the band intensity of each Arl3 in complex with UNC119 or BART and normalized to the same bands in Arl3-Q71L. We found that both fast cycling mutants, Arl3-D129N and Arl3-Y90C, had significantly higher levels than wild-type Arl3 (Figure 4E).
evidence: Quantitative data from in vivo crosslinking experiment shown in Figure 4E

claim: The relative amounts of effector complex formation correlate to migration phenotype.
source: The relative amounts of effector complex formation correlate to migration phenotype: wild-type has normal migration and is not significantly different than Arl3-T31N while the amount of Arl3-Y90C and Arl3-D129N activation is closer to Arl3-Q71L, resulting in defective migration.
evidence: Inference from comparison of effector binding levels and migration phenotypes

claim: The Y90C mutation maintains aberrant activity in the absence of GEF binding.
source: We also performed the in vivo crosslinking on cells expressing the Arl3-Y90C/R149H-FLAG double mutant construct to verify whether the aberrant activity of the fast cycling Y90C mutation is maintained in the absence of GEF binding. In Figure 4F, we see increased expression of the Arl3-UNC119 and Arl3-BART complexes in the Y90C/R149H double mutant compared to the R149H control.
evidence: Data from in vivo crosslinking experiment shown in Figure 4F

claim: GEF-independent nucleotide exchange to GTP is activating the Arl3-Y90C mutant in cells.
source: Together, these results confirm that GEF-independent nucleotide exchange to GTP is activating the Arl3-Y90C mutant in cells.
evidence: Inference from in vivo crosslinking data with Y90C/R149H double mutant

claim: In vivo crosslinking captured complexes between Arl13B-GFP and Arl3-Y90C showing that GEF binding is a feature of Arl3-Y90C in cells.
source: In contrast, in vivo crosslinking captured complexes between Arl13B-GFP and Arl3-Y90C showing that GEF binding is a feature of Arl3-Y90C in cells.
evidence: Data from in vivo crosslinking experiment shown in Figure 4G

claim: The Arl3-Y90C ability to tightly bind the GEF does not depend on its nucleotide status.
source: We also found Arl13B-GFP complexes with Arl3-T31N/Y90C, but not with Arl3-T31N, suggesting that the Arl3-Y90C ability to tightly bind the GEF does not depend on its nucleotide status (Figure 4G).
evidence: Data from in vivo crosslinking experiment shown in Figure 4G

claim: Wild-type Arl3-FLAG is activated by Arl13B-GFP as shown by the presence of UNC119 and BART complexes.
source: We found that wild-type Arl3-FLAG is activated by Arl13B-GFP shown by the presence of the UNC119 and BART complexes (Figure 5A).
evidence: Data from in vivo crosslinking experiment shown in Figure 5A

claim: In the presence of myc-tagged Arl3-Y90C or Arl3-T31N/Y90C, wild-type Arl3-FLAG no longer forms effector complexes.
source: However, in the presence of myc-tagged Arl3-Y90C or Arl3-T31N/Y90C, the wild-type Arl3-FLAG no longer forms these effector complexes (Figure 5A).
evidence: Data from in vivo crosslinking experiment shown in Figure 5A

claim: Wild-type Arl3 is unable to be activated in the presence of Arl3-Y90C.
source: These results show that wild-type Arl3 is unable to be activated in the presence of Arl3-Y90C, confirming our working model from Figure 4H.
evidence: Inference from in vivo crosslinking data

claim: Arl3-T31N/Y90C-FLAG did not result in a nuclear migration defect.
source: We then expressed the Arl3-T31N/Y90C-FLAG construct in mouse rod photoreceptors to test the migration phenotype in the absence of endogenous Arl3 activation and aberrant Arl3 activity, essentially mimicking a loss of function phenotype. We found that Arl3-T31N/Y90C-FLAG did not result in a nuclear migration defect (Figure 5B)
evidence: Data from in vivo electroporation shown in Figure 5B

claim: Arl3 activity is driving the disruption of nuclear migration in rods.
source: We found that Arl3-T31N/Y90C-FLAG did not result in a nuclear migration defect (Figure 5B), suggesting that Arl3 activity is driving the disruption of nuclear migration in rods (Figure 5C).
evidence: Inference from rescue experiment with T31N/Y90C double mutant

claim: Expression of UNC119-myc or Arl13B-GFP decreases the formation of active complexes between Arl3-Y90C-FLAG and endogenous effectors in cell culture.
source: In cell culture, we find that expression of either UNC119-myc or Arl13B-GFP decreases the formation of active complexes between Arl3-Y90C-FLAG and endogenous effectors (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Data from in vivo crosslinking experiment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Overexpressing the chaperones UNC119 and PDEδ with Arl3-Y90C-FLAG in mouse rods results in rod nuclei normally distributed throughout the ONL.
source: We tested this hypothesis in vivo by overexpressing the chaperones, UNC119 and PDEδ, with Arl3-Y90C-FLAG in mouse rods and found that rod nuclei were normally distributed throughout the ONL (Figure 6A).
evidence: Data from in vivo electroporation shown in Figure 6A

claim: When UNC119 or PDEδ were co-expressed with Arl3-Q71L, rod nuclei were still mislocalized.
source: Surprisingly, when UNC119 or PDEδ were co-expressed with Arl3-Q71L we found that rod nuclei were still mislocalized (Figure 6C).
evidence: Data from in vivo electroporation shown in Figure 6C

claim: Lower expression of Arl3-Q71L-FLAG still resulted in a rod migration defect.
source: The lower expression of Arl3-Q71L-FLAG still resulted in a rod migration defect; however, co-expression of PDEδ was now able to rescue the phenotype (Figure 6C).
evidence: Data from in vivo electroporation shown in Figure 6C

claim: Excess activation beyond a given threshold leads to an impairment in proper rod nuclear migration.
source: These data indicate that excess activation beyond a given threshold leads to an impairment in proper rod nuclear migration.
evidence: Inference from dose-dependent rescue experiments

claim: Co-expression of myc-INPP5E or NPHP3-myc rescued the Arl3-Y90C nuclear migration defect.
source: First, we co-expressed two different ciliary lipidated cargos, myc-INPP5E or NPHP3-myc, and found that they both rescued the Arl3-Y90C nuclear migration defect (Figure 7A).
evidence: Data from in vivo electroporation shown in Figure 7A

claim: Non-farnesylated INPP5E-C644A does not rescue the Arl3-Y90C migration defect.
source: We also tested non-farneslyated INPP5E-C644A, which has reduced binding to PDEδ (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) and found that the Arl3-Y90C migration defect persisted.
evidence: Data from in vivo electroporation shown in Figure 7A and pulldown data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claim: Cargo-chaperone binding is critical for rescue of the Arl3-Y90C migration defect.
source: This lipid dependency confirms that cargo-chaperone binding is critical for rescue.
evidence: Inference from comparison of lipidated and non-lipidated cargo rescue experiments

claim: Co-expression of myc-Rnd1 was unable to rescue the Arl3-Y90C nuclear migration defect.
source: Interestingly, we found that co-expression of myc-Rnd1 was unable to rescue the Arl3-Y90C nuclear migration defect (Figure 7A).
evidence: Data from in vivo electroporation shown in Figure 7A

claim: Only ciliary, chaperone-interacting cargo rescues the migration defect.
source: Together, our data show that only ciliary, chaperone-interacting cargo rescues the migration defect, which suggests that local increases in chaperone at the cilium may restore the Arl3 gradient in the cell by directly chelating Arl3-Y90C from Arl13B allowing endogenous Arl3 to activate normally (Figure 7B).
evidence: Inference from comparison of ciliary and non-ciliary cargo rescue experiments

claim: Arl3-Y90C/R149H double mutant maintains aberrant activity.
source: Our results show that a Arl3-Y90C/R149H double mutant maintains aberrant activity (Figure 4F) but is unable to bind to Arl13B (Figure 3A).
evidence: Data from in vivo crosslinking (Figure 4F) and co-immunoprecipitation (Figure 3A) experiments

claim: In vivo expression of Arl3-Y90C/R149H does not cause the migration defect.
source: In contrast to Arl3-Y90C, in vivo expression of Arl3-Y90C/R149H does not cause the migration defect, behaving similar to the Arl3-R149H single mutant (Figure 8B).
evidence: Data from in vivo electroporation shown in Figure 8B

claim: The ciliary gradient of active Arl3 is important for normal neuronal migration.
source: This result underscores the importance of the ciliary gradient of active Arl3 for normal neuronal migration.
evidence: Inference from Y90C/R149H rescue experiment

claim: Dominant Arl3 mutations result in increased active G-protein.
source: We discovered that dominant mutations result in increased active G-protein—Arl3-D67V has constitutive activity and Arl3-Y90C is fast cycling
evidence: Supported by biochemical data from the study

claim: Expression of dominant Arl3 mutations in mouse rods resulted in a displaced nuclear phenotype due to an aberrant Arl3-GTP gradient.
source: and their expression in mouse rods resulted in a displaced nuclear phenotype due to an aberrant Arl3-GTP gradient.
evidence: Supported by in vivo electroporation data from the study

claim: Removing or restoring the Arl3-GTP gradient within the cilium is sufficient to rescue the nuclear migration defect.
source: Using multiple strategies, we go on to show that removing or restoring the Arl3-GTP gradient within the cilium is sufficient to rescue the nuclear migration defect.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments with chaperones, cargo, and double mutants

claim: An Arl3 ciliary gradient is involved in proper positioning of photoreceptor nuclei during retinal development.
source: Together, our results reveal that an Arl3 ciliary gradient is involved in proper positioning of photoreceptor nuclei during retinal development.
evidence: Inference from all experimental data in the study

claim: Arl3-D67V forms a stable complex with RP2, similar to the constitutively active Q71L variant.
source: In fact, we found that Arl3-D67V forms a stable complex with RP2, similar to the constitutively active Q71L variant (Figure 4C)
evidence: Data from in vivo crosslinking experiment shown in Figure 4C

claim: Arl3-D67V disrupted UNC119 binding.
source: We also found that Arl3-D67V disrupted UNC119 binding (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Data from co-immunoprecipitation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Fast cycling mutations are dominant negative.
source: Our results highlight that fast cycling mutations are also dominant negative—normal activation of the endogenous GTPase is altered by Arl3-Y90C binding to Arl13B in the cilia.
evidence: Inference from Arl13B binding and rescue experiments

claim: The dominant negative feature of Arl3-Y90C was necessary but not sufficient to produce a migration defect.
source: Interestingly, while the dominant negative feature of Arl3-Y90C was necessary it was not sufficient to produce a migration defect suggesting that aberrant activity outside the cilia plays a role.
evidence: Inference from rescue experiments with Arl13B and Y90C/R149H double mutant

claim: The defect is not caused by an increase in overall Arl3 activity, but a disruption of proper Arl3-GTP localization within the cell.
source: Despite the higher levels of Arl3-Y90C activity in the cell, we actually find that reactivating endogenous Arl3 in the presence of this activity prevents the nuclear migration defect in rods. This suggests that the defect is not caused by an increase in overall Arl3 activity, but a disruption of proper Arl3-GTP localization within the cell.
evidence: Inference from rescue experiments

claim: More active Arl3 must be present in the cilium than the cell body for proper migration of rod nuclei during retinal development.
source: We demonstrate that more active Arl3 must be present in the cilium than the cell body for proper migration of rod nuclei during retinal development.
evidence: Inference from all experimental data showing gradient importance

claim: When Arl3 activity levels are increased in the cell body relative to the cilium, the driving force reverses, and cargo is no longer delivered.
source: When Arl3 activity levels are increased in the cell body relative to the cilium, the driving force reverses, and cargo is no longer delivered.
evidence: Speculation based on gradient model

claim: Disrupting delivery of cargo might result in downregulation of the cargo.
source: It is possible that disrupting delivery results in downregulation of the cargo.
evidence: Speculation about mechanism

claim: Absence of Arl3 activity does not cause a migration defect because there would be no driving force on the cargo and its widespread delivery could result in sufficient accumulation at the cilium.
source: This might explain why absence of Arl3 activity does not cause a migration defect (Figure 5), as there would be no driving force on the cargo and its widespread delivery could result in sufficient accumulation at the cilium.
evidence: Speculation to explain T31N/Y90C result

claim: RP2 gene therapy in adult mice slowed degeneration, suggesting that the rod nuclear mislocalization may not be pathogenic.
source: However, RP2 gene therapy in adult mice slowed degeneration, suggesting that the rod nuclear mislocalization may not be pathogenic (Li et al., 2013; Mookherjee et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 2013; Mookherjee et al., 2015

claim: Basal displacement of rod nuclei coincides with retinal dysfunction including defects in synapse formation.
source: Nevertheless, it was previously shown that basal displacement of rod nuclei coincides with retinal disfunction including defects in synapse formation (Aghaizu et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to Aghaizu et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2011

claim: Mutations in Arl13B, the Arl3 GEF, cause the syndromic ciliopathy Joubert syndrome.
source: In fact, mutations in Arl13B, the Arl3 GEF, cause the syndromic ciliopathy Joubert syndrome (Cantagrel et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to Cantagrel et al., 2008

claim: Mutations in Arl13B can cause a reduction of Arl3 activation.
source: and can cause a reduction of Arl3 activation (Gotthardt et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gotthardt et al., 2015

claim: The Arl3 GAP RP2 causes non-syndromic retinal degeneration.
source: The Arl3 GAP RP2, on the other hand, causes non-syndromic retinal degeneration (Breuer et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by citation to Breuer et al., 2002

claim: The impact of excess active Arl3 on cells is more detrimental for retinal photoreceptors than other ciliated cells throughout the body.
source: providing more evidence that the impact of excess active Arl3 on cells is more detrimental for retinal photoreceptors than other ciliated cells throughout the body.
evidence: Inference from comparison of RP2 and Arl13B disease phenotypes

claim: Primary cilia have been shown to play a role in neuronal nuclear migration in the brain.
source: In the brain, primary cilia have previously been shown to play a role in neuronal nuclear migration, with studies implicating both Arl13B (Higginbotham et al., 2012) and cAMP signaling (Stoufflet et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Higginbotham et al., 2012 and Stoufflet et al., 2020
